candidates.title: How metaverse influencers shape electronic word-of-mouth: Credibility, attractiveness, and parasocial relationships across cultures and gender
candidates.abstract: Metaverse Influencers (MVIs) are technologically constructed social actors increasingly promoting tourism destinations. However, they continue to be viewed as uncannily or authentically fake, raising questions about whether followers perceive them as credible, form meaningful parasocial relationships with them, and intend to recommend the destinations they endorse. To address these gaps, this study integrated source credibility theory, parasocial relationship theory, and the similarity-attractiveness model and tested a framework linking source credibility and physical attractiveness to e-WOM intentions, with parasocial relationship as the mediator. Using a quantitative design across three cases (main effects/mediation; UK–USA–India; female–male), results showed that parasocial relationships increased e-WOM, and source credibility increased both parasocial relationships and e-WOM. Physical attractiveness did not directly increase e-WOM, but strengthened parasocial relationships, which fully mediated the attractiveness–e-WOM link; mediation was partial for credibility. Only one cross-country difference emerged (attractiveness to e-WOM was stronger in the USA), and one gender difference (attractiveness to parasocial relationship stronger for males). These findings show that the extent to which MVIs influence their followers is not only dependent upon the designed appearance of the MVI itself but also on whether followers perceive them as credible and develop parasocial relationships with them. The study enhances our knowledge of human relationships with synthetic social actors and provides insights into how MVIs should be created to responsibly promote tourism communications.

candidates.title: OpenWater Hub: An open-source hardware platform for marine robotics support and water quality data acquisition
candidates.abstract: At present, there is no single open-source electronic hardware platform that natively integrates 24 V industrial RS485 sensors with marine robotic and hydroponic actuation. Consequently, hardware fragmentation exists severely in underwater sensing and environmental monitoring. Researchers using benchtop calibration must purchase closed-source ecosystems with proprietary operating systems, limiting the use of custom control loops. Conversely, open-source embedded systems provide optimized low-voltage passive monitoring but lack sufficient power for heavy actuators.The OpenWater Hub (OWH) provides a centralized platform for these two areas to exist on one printed circuit board (PCB). The PCB features a 24 V pass-through bus that supports the heavy inrush currents of industrial RS485 probes. A dual-ATmega128A topology is utilized to prevent serial polling delays from disrupting real-time motor control. The architecture consists of one chip that isolates Modbus communication for sub-millisecond parsing, and another chip that drives soft robotic fish and actuators via four 3.0 A PWM channels.The core board is configured to transform across four deployment variants: a benchtop logger, a portable field laboratory, an autonomous floating station, and a tethered robotic support hub. Modular UART sockets support telemetry via LoRa, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and cellular modules. The static baseline power consumption was 196.4 mW; after 240 hours of thermal testing, the OWH demonstrated > 99.97% telemetry reliability and logged chemical validations yielding a 0.9903 correlation coefficient value. Documentation and C++ logic files for the reproduction of all deployment variants are included.

candidates.title: Brain-computer interfaces in pediatric populations: research advances, application challenges, and future directions
candidates.abstract: Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) establish direct communication pathways between the brain and external devices. Leveraging the unique neuroplasticity of the developing brain, BCIs have emerged as a novel rehabilitative technology for children with neurodevelopmental disorders, including cerebral palsy, autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and perinatal brain injury. This review comprehensively examines five major BCI paradigms—P300, motor imagery (MI), steady-state visual evoked potentials (SSVEP), functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), and multimodal hybrid systems—with respect to their pediatric adaptability, technical limitations, and optimization strategies. We summarize the existing evidence across four key clinical applications: augmentative and alternative communication (AAC), motor function rehabilitation, ADHD attention training, and ASD social–emotional intervention. Key intrinsic (cognitive and physiological) and extrinsic (device and environmental) variables affecting BCI performance in children are analyzed, along with general optimization approaches including personalized parameter tuning, pre-training neurofeedback, and lightweight hardware modifications. Furthermore, we examine multilayer barriers to pediatric BCI adoption, including user experience, clinical workforce readiness, translational pathways, and child-specific ethical considerations. Preliminary evidence suggests that non-invasive BCIs can be feasibly used in children above 5 years of age, although this finding is based on short-term studies with small sample sizes and requires further validation through larger longitudinal trials. However, the immature pediatric brain, short attention spans, and low device tolerance preclude direct translation of adult BCI systems. While evidence is more established for AAC and motor rehabilitation in cerebral palsy, large-scale long-term data are still lacking for ADHD and ASD interventions. Future efforts should prioritize child-specific lightweight wearable devices, multicenter longitudinal trials, immersive integration with virtual reality (VR) and social robots, standardized clinical service frameworks, and ethical guidelines for invasive pediatric BCIs, thereby facilitating the transition of BCI technology from laboratory to clinical and home settings and maximizing its value in promoting neurodevelopmental plasticity in children with special needs.

candidates.title: Toward intelligent safety assurance in construction human-robot collaboration
candidates.abstract: Construction human-robot collaboration (HRC) introduces physical, ergonomic, and cognitive risks that conventional isolated-based safeguards cannot adequately manage in dynamic, unstructured worksites and requires more adaptive forms of safety assurance. Although diverse robotics-related approaches have been developed, how they function as interconnected, active safety-assurance mechanisms for construction HRC remains insufficiently synthesised. This paper systematically reviews 215 studies published from 2011 to 2025 through PRISMA-guided screening, bibliometric analysis and thematic synthesis. Five connected technological directions are identified: robot design optimisation, context-aware perception, human-centric understanding and forecasting, autonomous robotic adaptation, and safety management. The synthesis shows a transition from passive risk avoidance toward perception-driven, prediction, and adaptive safety assurance, but 54% of studies remain limited to controlled laboratory validation, and few integrate uncertainty across sensing, prediction, control and supervision. Accordingly, a closed-loop framework is proposed to guide the integration and construction-realistic validation of verifiable, uncertainty-aware HRC safety systems.

candidates.title: Deep-MultiAPP: First-impression based apparent personality trait prediction from short videos with multimodal deep learning
candidates.abstract: Abstract Automated Apparent Personality Prediction (APP) from multimodal data holds significant promise for enhancing Human-Computer Interactions (HCIs), yet existing models often fall short in effectively fusing diverse cues like visual expressions, audio prosody, and textual semantics, leading to suboptimal accuracy and interpretability in real-world applications. This study introduces Deep-MultiAPP, a novel multimodal deep learning architecture designed to address these limitations by integrating Residual Network (ResNet-50) and Vision Transformer (ViT-B/16) for hybrid visual feature extraction, Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) for temporal modeling, enhanced audio Multilayer Perceptrons (MLPs) for incorporating mean-pooled log-Mel spectrograms, and Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) for text embeddings with late decision-level fusion combines modality-specific regressors (weights: vision 0.6, audio 0.3, text 0.1). On the ChaLearn First Impressions V2 dataset, Deep-MultiAPP achieved a state-of-the-art mean regression accuracy of 91.77% across the Big-Five traits, outperforming prior baselines by ∼0.25–0.47%. Binarized classification at a 0.5 threshold yielded a macro-averaged precision of 79.54%, recall of 80.13%, and F1-score of 79.83%, as validated by confusion matrices showing balanced error distributions despite class imbalances. These results demonstrate Deep-MultiAPP's superior capability in capturing nuanced personality cues, paving the way for more reliable artificial intelligence (AI) systems in fields like recruitment, mental health screening, and social robotics, while highlighting the need for bias audits and cross-cultural validations to ensure equitable deployment for responsible real-world use.

candidates.title: SMaRTAban: a voice-controlled LLM agent for quadruped mobile robotics with integrated vision
candidates.abstract: Abstract Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as powerful tools for enabling intuitive human-robot interaction through natural language. However, existing approaches often lack evaluated voice control in languages other than English, integrated vision, and comprehensive safety mechanisms. We present SMaRTAban (Smart Multi-legged Robotic Transformer Agent Artaban), a system that combines a LangGraph ReAct agent with the quadruped mobile robot Artaban for natural language control. Our system integrates: (1) voice commands with automatic language detection via Whisper, evaluated on English and Slovak, (2) on-demand scene interpretation via GPT-4o vision, (3) a safety-focused system prompt with interruptible tool execution, and (4) a React-based GUI for transparent operation monitoring. A pilot voice-control evaluation on 120 samples showed robust semantic understanding across English and Slovak (BERTScore F1: 0.87–1.00), despite transcription challenges in Slovak. We further conducted 4,800 accepted tool-calling trials across two models, six agent and prompting configurations, two languages, and 10 command scenarios. The strongest configuration combined iterative ReAct execution, an explicit system prompt, and few-shot prompting with three task-specific movement examples, achieving a tool-call F1 of 0.9977 and 96.5% exact-sequence success with GPT-4o. A separate performance evaluation showed that remote transcription and model processing dominated response time, whereas local ROS communication contributed only a few milliseconds.

candidates.title: Spontaneous visual perspective-taking in human–robot interaction as a methodological artifact of spatial stimulus arrangement
candidates.abstract: Abstract While prior research has demonstrated spontaneous visual perspective-taking (VPT) towards robots using static images or videos of existing robots, little is known about whether VPT occurs with robotic avatars or in immersive environments like virtual reality (VR). The purpose of this research was to extend the existing research to robotic avatars and VR as a medium for interaction. Study 1 confirmed that participants spontaneously adopt the perspective of both robotic and human avatars in static images, with no significant difference in VPT between the two agents. Study 2 compared VPT in video and VR conditions, revealing unexpectedly higher VPT in the video condition, despite VR’s greater sense of copresence. We suspected that the spatial context of stimulus presentation played a critical role. Therefore, Study 3 further explored this by manipulating the placement of stimuli in the robot’s versus the shared environment, revealing that VPT was higher when stimuli were presented exclusively in the robot’s environment. This finding suggests that earlier VPT research may have a critical methodological limitation, as it did not account for spatial context in real human–robot interaction scenarios, which could limit its applicability to real-world robot interactions.

candidates.title: A review of full-stack autonomous obstacle avoidance for assistive robots for the disabled
candidates.abstract: With the intensification of population aging and the increasing awareness of protecting the rights of the disabled, significant progress has been made in assistive robots for visually impaired people, the mobility impairments and other groups. Research in this field focuses on four key technical dimensions: environmental perception, obstacle recognition and classification, path planning and obstacle avoidance algorithms, and scenario-based applications. This analysis particularly focuses on the ability of multi-sensor fusion to acquire spatial information in complex and dynamic environments, and reviews the technological evolution in target detection, semantic understanding, and passable area determination. The work further explores algorithms ranging from global path planning to local obstacle avoidance strategies, as well as reinforcement learning and multi-algorithm integration. Furthermore, this narrative review synthesizes the current research on assistive technologies, including guide robots for the visually impaired, intelligent mobility platforms for wheelchair users, and solutions adaptable to both indoor and outdoor environments. The insights derived from this review offer a reliable foundation to support the travel and daily activities of people with disabilities.

candidates.title: Knowledge- and memory-based interactive task learning for human robot collaboration
candidates.abstract: This work proposes a novel framework for interactive task learning that combines essential task knowledge with experiential tuning, a combination we need for cognition-inspired learning for robots. Interactive task learning is an approach inspired by research on cognitive development that promotes story-based memory structures for learning the essence of a task, which are extended and optimized over time by experiences. The proposed framework combines two recent approaches: (1) deploying actionable knowledge graphs (AKGs) as a knowledge base to help robots understand and generalize tasks and (2) integrating Narrative-Enabled Episodic Memories (NEEMs) as semantic and explainable memory structures for experiences. We integrate AKGs into the NEEM structure to benefit from the actionable function description as part of a structure that improves by ongoing and consecutive interactions. If robots grasp the essence of a task, they can transfer knowledge to similar ones. For example, they can use the knowledge of “cutting bread” to “slicing a cucumber,” distinguishing between similar tasks like cutting and slicing, but also reasoning about the similarity of needed tools and motions. Our framework links the existing concepts AKGs and NEEMs in a scenario of task demonstrations for robots to reason about semantic task and object information. By inferring task parameters like cut positions, pour angles, and stop conditions directly from AKGs, robots can achieve task generalization across diverse actions. Our example study setup for the proposed model illustrates this for household tasks, focusing on fruit-cutting and pouring. This is a hypothesis paper: we present the framework and two planned study designs, and we do not report robot experiments or task-success measurements. An example NEEM can be accessed and queried on the resource website 1 .

candidates.title: Videogame spectatorship and orbital fandom value
candidates.abstract: This thesis examines the layered and evolving nature of online videogame fandoms, with a particular focus on what it terms orbital fandom; fan communities that emerged one or more step removed from the original game text.Rather than engaging directly with the game itself, these fans form attachment through derivative content, content creators, and platform-medicated interactions.By shifting attention to these decentralised forms of engagement, the thesis expands existing models of fandom to account for the complex social, affective, and economic dynamics that shape participation in contemporary digital game cultures.To explore these dynamics, the research draws on a mixed-methods approach combining virtual ethnography, semi-structured stakeholder interviews, and a participant journaling study.This methodology allows for both creator-and viewercentred perspectives, capturing how value; cultural, social, and monetary is produced, circulated, and contested within platformed fan ecosystems.The thesis develops the Orbital Fandom Framework, a conceptual model that articulates how these forms of fandom operate within the wider infrastructures of platform governance and digital labour.Empirical findings reveal how fan labour often takes place under informal, precarious, and frequently unacknowledged conditions.At the same time, fan contributions, particularly within orbital fandoms, play a vital role in shaping visibility, community cohesion, and even commercial success within the games industry.The thesis also explores the emotional intensities of parasocial relationships and the ethical concerns surrounding platform incentives and exploitation.These findings hold relevance not only for academic debates in game and fan studies but also for developers and platform designers seeking to engage with fan communities in more ethical and inclusive ways.By introducing a new conceptual vocabulary, advancing a critical framework, and offering practical insights, this research contributes to a deeper understanding of the socio-cultural and economic life of videogame fandoms in the platform era.

candidates.title: The Failure Is in the Readout: Fine-Grained Emotion Recognition Benchmarks Measure Elicitation, Not Perception
candidates.abstract: Fine-grained emotion recognition supports therapy tools and social robots, but it needs facial data, which raises privacy and data-protection concerns. EmoNet-Face-HQ answers that with generated portraits, expert-rated over a $40$-category taxonomy far finer than the usual six to eight basic emotions. Under the protocol it ships with, vision-language models (VLMs) score poorly on that taxonomy, and the benchmark concludes that a dedicated fine-tuned model is necessary: Empathic-Insight-Face (EIF; Small/Large). We show that off-the-shelf VLMs match or beat that fine-tuned model when the answer is not generated but read from the logits, as one binary query per category. We keep the benchmark's images, taxonomy and ratings, and change only how the answer is read. Experts agree at $κ_w = 0.468$ on the five categories they measure most reliably. Generatively, no interval among eleven open-weight VLMs lies entirely above that anchor ($κ_w=0.268$-$0.486$). Under verification all eleven clear it, each of them significantly better at $κ_w=0.507$-$0.586$. Three also significantly beat EIF sitting at $κ_w = 0.551$ (Small; $0.534$ Large). The gain comes from the graded probability and not from asking a yes/no question: as a control, thresholding those same probabilities to yes/no costs 142% of the average gains and drops binarization below generative elicitation to $κ_w=0.254$-$0.423$. A replication on real photographs (FACES) is weaker and mixed: of the ten models that pass a validity gate, six gain, three are neutral to positive and one is negative, so the effect is not confined to synthetic data.

candidates.title: Robotic Pet or Soft Toy? An Autoethnographic Study of Living with MetaCat in the Home
candidates.abstract: Lifelike robotic cats, covered in soft fur and sensor-embedded, are now commercially available and being targeted at home settings. Typically, they are designed to respond to human touch and voice with pet-like behaviours such as purring, meowing and tail wagging. This ambivalence between pet-like form and robotic features raises questions about how they will integrate into home life. Will family members treat them like pets, toys or something else? Research has focused on their use for health and aged care but less so on everyday use in families. We conducted an autoethnography combined with observations in which nine researcher-participants with diverse backgrounds, ages and life settings spent up to ten days each with a robot cat called MetaCat. Our findings elicited surprising, sometimes contradictory experiences and feelings. We report on where MetaCat was placed in the home and the interactions it triggered. We discuss benefits, tensions and design implications when developing pet-like versus robot-like products.

candidates.title: Hotel service robots as experiential touchpoints: a modified robotic TOCE model
candidates.abstract: This study applies the Tourist On-site Co-creation Experience (TOCE) framework to examine how hotel service robots shape guest experience in a non-human service context. Drawing on value co-creation and human-robot interaction perspectives, the study explores how robot-mediated encounters become part of on-site hotel experience formation. A total of 438 online reviews from hotels that have adopted service robots were analyzed using a two-stage approach combining Leximancer 5.0 and manual thematic analysis. The findings show that robot encounters generally follow a main value co-creation pathway, in which robots stimulate curiosity, active participation, playful novelty, and social interactions. Robots function not only as service tools, but also as experiential touchpoints within the hotel stay. At the same time, this co-created value is fragile and may shift toward co-destruction under specific boundary conditions, including functional incompetence, embodiment-related discomfort, and service disruption. Based on these findings, the study proposes a Modified Robotic TOCE Model that explains how robot encounters move through a dual-pathway process of co-creation and conditional failure. The study contributes to hospitality and tourism research by extending TOCE to robot-mediated service encounters and offers practical implications for hotel robot design, deployment, and service delivery.

candidates.title: No universal patient: temporal logics of harm prevention in emotional AI healthcare across Japan, China, and Hong Kong
candidates.abstract: Abstract Across East Asia, emotional AI in healthcare is governed through markedly different normative and institutional rationalities that construct the patient, harm, and vulnerability in distinct ways. This article develops a triadic analytical framework, integrating moral anthropologies, models of legitimacy, and regulatory instruments, to examine governance rationalities in Japan, China, and Hong Kong. Instead of treating Asian perspectives as variations on Euro-American principlism, this analysis examines these jurisdictions in their own right, showing how each constructs the patient differently, as relational node, protected subject, or rights-holder, and prioritises different harms accordingly. Using PARO, a therapeutic companion robot deployed globally in elderly care, as a stylised analytical device, the article shows that the same robot becomes three different regulatory objects. This case study surfaces a fourth dimension of governance rationality: temporal orientation. Japan’s governance rationality is iterative, allowing norms to emerge through use and professional dialogue; China’s is preventive, anticipating and regulating harms before deployment; and Hong Kong’s is reactive, adjudicating violations after they occur. These temporal orientations shape harm-prevention outcomes as consequentially as the choice of instruments, and constitute the article’s primary empirical contribution. Extending Cheong’s analysis of structural accountability gaps and Zuboff’s account of how institutional power determines which technological harms become actionable, the comparison suggests that vulnerability, harm, and accountability function as governance-produced categories rather than as properties inherent to the technology. The article argues that governing emotional AI requires not harmonisation of principles but recognition of ontological difference, an epistemological reorientation with direct implications for transnational governance frameworks.

candidates.title: ARAM: a threshold model for understanding occupant acceptance of architectural robot adaptations
candidates.abstract: Physical interior elements are increasingly becoming roboticised to support occupant needs. Partitions, ceilings, and furniture can now physically and autonomously change shape or move to architecturally “adapt” indoor spaces, with the aim of improving occupant comfort, satisfaction, and wellbeing. However, occupants sometimes reject these adaptations when they are perceived as disruptive, unpredictable, or difficult to control. Motivated by the goal of making architectural robots more acceptable, we involved an interdisciplinary team of experts in human-building interaction, human-robot interaction, psychology, anthropology, and human comfort to qualitatively re-analyze how occupants accepted adaptations across three previous studies on robotic partitions. We found that an occupant tended to accept an adaptation when they recognized a personal need that the architectural robot was capable of addressing in a socially justifiable way. Accordingly, we developed the Architectural Robot Acceptance Model (ARAM), in which three qualitative thresholds along a continuum of perceived stress severity define four distinct acceptance responses to a specific adaptation. As the positions of these thresholds may vary across occupants and situations, ARAM supports testable estimates of how an occupant may respond to different appraisal states of personal need, adaptation capability, and social justification. Because architectural robot adaptations may simultaneously be experienced as robotic behaviors, building automation, and socially situated environmental adjustments, ARAM is particularly relevant to individual adaptations that enter occupants' spatial experience and may affect co-located others. We then discuss how the model can inform situated estimates of occupant acceptance of architectural robot adaptations, and outline how its broader relevance to other robotic, automated, intelligent, and smart technologies embedded in the built environment may be evaluated in future work.

candidates.title: Disclosure willingness anthropomorphism and thinking style shape perceived fit and comfort in AI mental health chatbot interactions
candidates.abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (AI) conversational agents are increasingly used for everyday, non-clinical mental-health support, yet little is known about when these exchanges feel fitting and comfortable. We used a laboratory mixed-methods design to examine associations among perceived convenience of interaction (PCI), relational attitude (RA), willingness to self-disclose (WSD), anthropomorphism (AN), perceived fit/comfort (FC), and thinking style in 83 participants (43 rational-dominant; 40 experiential-dominant). WSD showed the strongest unique association with FC. A post hoc reverse model also found a unique FC-WSD association, leaving their temporal order unresolved. AN had no stable direct association with FC, but the WSD-FC association became stronger as AN increased. Group comparisons and continuous Rational-Experiential Inventory (REI) analyses converged: relatively stronger experiential processing was associated with higher AN, whereas relatively stronger rational processing was associated with higher WSD. The group-blind thematic analysis linked disclosure decisions to privacy, control, social distance, functional usefulness, and affective comfort. Together, the findings identify WSD as a key correlate of FC and show that anthropomorphism conditions this association rather than simply improving the interaction. Clear boundaries, controllability, and adjustable relational cues therefore warrant attention in future design research.

candidates.title: Can there really be ethical robots for autistic children?
candidates.abstract: Abstract With the advancement of autonomous technologies such as AI-driven social robots, the academic discussions around ethical standards have intensified over the years. These discussions have resulted in increased emphasis on concepts such as safety, trust, privacy, human dignity and well-being along with variety of ethical frameworks proposed by scholars. In parallel with these technological developments, therapeutic interventions for autistic children assisted by AI and social robots have also attracted increased attention. Against this backdrop, this paper critically examines six social robotics projects funded under the EU’s Horizon 2020 initiative from an ethics perspective. The main aim of these completed projects was to develop AI-driven semi-autonomous technologies such as humanoid and non-humanoid robots to assist autism interventions. To address the ethical shortcomings of the said projects, this paper mobilizes perspectives from critical disability studies, critical autism studies and the autism community itself, particularly concerning the negative impact of interventions on autistic individuals as a neurominority group. Beyond the commonly addressed shortcomings in the field of AI and social robotics, the article highlights that the biggest shortcoming of these projects is the absence of critical reflection on the ethical acceptability of applying neuronormative behavioral interventions to a neurominority group. By situating robot-assisted interventions within the context of normalization and technoableism, the article points out the epistemic injustice and the harm that can be potentially enacted on autistic people through such technologically aided interventions. Ultimately, the paper questions whether ethical assistive technologies for autistic individuals can exist under these circumstances.

candidates.title: Service Robotics: Human-Centered Architectures, Safety Constraints, and Reliability Modeling
candidates.abstract: This open-access educational module presents the architectural frameworks, safety clearance constraints, compliance mechanics, and reliability models foundational to modern service robotics. Core Technical Topics Functional System Architecture: Subsystem decomposition spanning multi-modal perception (RGB-D, LiDAR), real-time SLAM pose estimation, behavior tree task planning, and compliant manipulation. State-Space Dynamics: Discrete-time kinematic and dynamic transition modeling (x_(k+1) = f(x_k, u_k) + w_k) and stochastic sensor correction. Human-Aware Navigation & Safety Constraints: Pedestrian spatial separation boundaries (||p_r(t) - p_h(t)|| >= d_safe), dynamic obstacle deceleration profiles, and social force proxemics. Human–Robot Interaction (HRI): Maximum a posteriori (MAP) Bayesian speech command decoding (a = argmax_k P(k | s)), multi-modal intent disambiguation, and acoustic beamforming. Physical Compliance & Impact Safety: Contact force boundaries (F <= F_max), Series Elastic Actuation (SEA), structural yielding compliance (delta_max = F_max / k_arm), and ISO 13482 safety standards for personal care robots. Energy Management & System Reliability: Battery operating endurance modeling (t_op = E / P), constant failure rate models (lambda), exponential mission survival probability (R(t) = exp(-lambda*t)), and Mean Time Between Failures (MTBF = 1 / lambda). Pedagogical Assets 12 fully worked numerical engineering problems with complete mathematical derivations and step-by-step solutions. Dedicated engineering challenges analysis addressing pedestrian "freezing robot" bottlenecks, acoustic reverberation in public spaces, multi-floor IoT elevator integration, and biomechanical collision boundaries. Interactive conceptual quick reviews and self-assessment checkpoints. Standardized layout suitable for university coursework adoption and permanent reference. Target Audience & Level Designed for upper-division undergraduate engineering courses (Robotics, Mechatronics, Systems Engineering, and Human–Robot Interaction), advanced university-preparatory STEM programs, and service robot systems engineers.

candidates.title: Future of edge AI in biodiversity monitoring
candidates.abstract: Abstract Many ecological decisions are slowed by the gap between collecting and analysing biodiversity information. Edge computing moves data processing closer to the sensor, with edge artificial intelligence (AI) using AI models for data processing and selective data transfer. edge AI extends the scope of biodiversity monitoring by complementing retrospective ecological analysis with real‐time sensing, enabling responsive and adaptive decision‐making. However, the adoption of edge AI systems in ecological research remains fragmented because deploying efficient and reliable systems is complex. Edge hardware, on‐device AI models and network configuration are tightly linked, such that optimising any one component shapes the performance and feasibility of the others, demanding holistic system design. For the uptake of edge AI in biodiversity monitoring, it is essential to understand the design trade‐offs, performance constraints and implementation challenges faced by current systems. Here, we analyse 82 studies published between 2017 and 2025 that use edge AI systems for biodiversity monitoring across acoustic, vision‐based, tracking and multi‐modal sensing. We synthesise hardware platforms, AI model optimisation and wireless communication to assess how these design choices influence ecological inference and determine the practicality and longevity of field deployments. Annual publications rise moderately from 3 in 2017 to 19 in 2025. Across these studies, we identify four system types that represent distinct patterns of edge computing adoption in ecological monitoring. These include low‐power microcontrollers (MCUs) for single‐taxon or rare‐event detection ( Type I: TinyML ), single‐board computers (SBCs) supporting multi‐species classification and real‐time alerts ( Type II: edge AI ), distributed systems coordinating processing across multiple devices ( Type III: Distributed edge AI ) and network‐connected devices for cloud processing ( Type IV: Cloud AI ). Each type illustrates different trade‐offs among power consumption, computational capability and communication requirements. Our analysis reveals the evolution of edge AI systems from proof‐of‐concept to robust, scalable tools. We argue that edge AI systems enable timely and scalable ecological observations, but realising their full potential depends on closer collaboration between ecologists, engineers and data scientists to align AI model development and system design with ecological needs and field realities.

candidates.title: Foundations of Robotics
candidates.abstract: This book introduces readers to graduate-level study of robotics through an integrated, interdisciplinary approach that spans mechatronics, control theory, computer science, and AI. It is designed to unite students from these fields, equipping them with the collaborative skills needed to excel in robotics. It is structured around three core pillars: Mechatronics , Cybernetics , and AI . Mechatronics introduces practical tools and materials for robot building, programming, and design, covering open-source hardware, sensors, actuators, embedded systems like ESP32, and middleware like ROS2. Cybernetics explores feedback, control, kinematics, and dynamics, enabling the execution of complex trajectories for robots such as drones, mobile robots, and robotic arms, grounded in linear algebra and Lagrangian mechanics. AI explores modern transformer-based models, including GPTs and diffusion models, teaching robots to perceive, learn, and plan using Bayesian probability, neural networks, and PyTorch programming. Together, these sections provide a comprehensive foundation for understanding and innovating in robotics. Bridging foundational theory and real-world applications, this book is core course reading for advanced undergraduate and graduate students of robotics, mechatronics, and artificial intelligence. It is also a valuable resource for maker communities, equipping them with the skills needed to succeed in this cutting-edge field.

candidates.title: Personalizing Older Adults’ Cognitive Training Robot Games with LLM Support
candidates.abstract: As populations age, innovative solutions are needed to support cognitive health in older adults. This paper presents a platform that delivers personalized cognitive training games through a humanoid robot, leveraging a Large Language Model (LLM) to generate game content and users’ profiles from autobiographical memories. Four serious games were designed and developed as cognitive-stimulation activities, with content dynamically tailored to user profiles to provide personalised exercises. We conducted a four-week feasibility and user-experience evaluation study with 20 older adults (65+) and interviews with 10 caregivers to assess system’s usability, emotional impact, and perceived value. Results show that participants found the robot-delivered games engaging and emotionally meaningful, with significant improvement in perceived user control and high usability ratings. Caregivers especially valued the LLMs’ potential for scalable personalization. This work highlights the feasibility of integrating LLMs and social robots for cognitive activities in aging populations, providing indications on how to achieve this.

candidates.title: Large language model attributes and perceived moral agency of artificial moral advisors
candidates.abstract: Introduction Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used as conversational artificial moral advisors capable of providing ethical guidance, moral reflection, and recommendations regarding complex moral dilemmas. Despite their ability to generate coherent and persuasive moral discourse, LLMs lack genuine moral understanding, intentionality, and reflective judgment, raising concerns that users may overattribute moral agency to these systems. Drawing on Theory of Mind, AI Moral Agency, and the Godspeed framework, this study investigates how perceived LLM attributes—namely anthropomorphism, animacy, likeability, and intelligence—are associated with users' perceptions of agency and morality in the context of artificial moral advisors. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted with 758 valid respondents who were presented with vignette-based moral dilemmas relevant to young adults and instructed to imagine seeking advice from LLM-based conversational agents. Results Perceived agency was positively associated with perceived morality, suggesting that users are more likely to regard LLM-based artificial moral advisors as morally capable when they perceive them as autonomous, intentional, and self-directed entities. Perceived LLM anthropomorphism and animacy were significantly and positively associated with perceived agency, with perceived agency fully mediating their associations with the perceived morality of artificial moral advisors. Perceived LLM likeability and intelligence were positively associated with perceived morality but were not significantly associated with perceived agency, suggesting that users may infer moral capability from social appeal and cognitive competence without necessarily attributing autonomy or intentionality to these systems. Discussion These findings offer important theoretical and practical implications for the ethical design of artificial moral advisors, particularly regarding the need to prevent inflated perceptions of AI moral competence and authority.

candidates.title: ISEED: an always-on cognitive architecture for experience-driven interaction-oriented humanoid robots
candidates.abstract: Current cognitive architectures for social robots, even when conceived as autonomous and adaptable, remain largely grounded in fully digital, von Neumann-style paradigms, where acquired knowledge is detached from individual experience. This contrasts with biological cognition, in which learning emerges from continuous, embodied interaction which leads to personal, non-copyable competencies. In this perspective, we argue that achieving truly adaptive and socially situated robotic agents requires a paradigm shift toward hybrid, bio-inspired, always-on architectures, where dynamic, and digitally implementable components coexist. Such architecture supports continuous activity, structural plasticity, and experience-dependent learning, enabling knowledge to emerge and strengthen from distributed interactions rather than from copiable parameters. We outline a roadmap in which embodiment, dynamical systems, endogenous values, and socially grounded learning mechanisms are central design principles of such cognitive architecture, and we discuss how these ideas can scale beyond sensorimotor skills toward what we believe being important for social robots. These principles are currently being explored in a bioinspired initiative (iCog) aimed at developing the ISEED (Interaction-oriented Situated Embodied Experience-Driven) cognitive architecture, a framework for humanoid social robots, meant to be a testbed for implementing and validating a hybrid, experience-driven approach for real-world cooperative robot partners.

candidates.title: Robotic servers, baristas and bartenders: a systematic review and framework
candidates.abstract: Purpose As robots proliferate across food and beverage (F&B) services, from robotic servers and baristas to kitchen assistants and bartenders, understanding human–robot interaction in these contexts has become critical for both industry and academia. The purpose of this study is to synthesize existing literature on service robots within F&B contexts. Design/methodology/approach The review uses the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines and the Context–Intervention–Mechanisms–Outcomes (CIMO) framework to extract and synthesize findings from 180 peer-reviewed studies. Findings The synthesis identifies five key themes: robot attributes and design; value creation; service failure and recovery; consumer and service format contingencies; and barriers to adoption. Three critical gaps emerged: insufficient differentiation between restaurant types, lack of specification of robot service roles and limited integration of different value perspectives specific to the nature of F&B businesses. Research limitations/implications This review advances human–robot interaction research by identifying four categories of robotic intervention cues (role, positioning, design and communication), which provide a theoretically grounded architecture for organizing future research in F&B contexts. Theoretical gaps and future research directions are also provided, especially with regard to beverage and culinary production, value for money, price fairness and robo-tipping. Originality/value This review establishes F&B robotics as a theoretically distinct stream within hospitality and tourism service robot research and offers a CIMO-based framework for explaining how robotized service encounters shape consumer responses in F&B contexts.

candidates.title: Affordance-based robot manipulation with flow matching
candidates.abstract: We present a framework for assistive robot manipulation that addresses two fundamental challenges: efficient adaptation of large-scale models for scene affordance understanding and effective learning of robot actions by grounding the visual affordance. To tackle the first challenge, we adopt a parameter-efficient prompt tuning method, prepending learnable text prompts to a frozen vision model to predict affordances, while considering spatial and semantic relationships in multi-task scenarios. For the second challenge, we propose a flow matching method, representing a robot visuomotor policy as a conditional process of flowing random waypoints to desired robot actions. We introduce a real-world dataset with 10 tasks to evaluate our approach. Experiments show our prompt tuning method achieves competitive or superior performance to other finetuning protocols across data scales, while satisfying parameter efficiency. Furthermore, flow matching yields more stable training and faster inference compared to diffusion policy; specifically, 1-step flow matching achieves comparable accuracy to 16-step DDIM while reducing inference time by roughly 85%. Our framework seamlessly unifies high-level parameter-efficient affordance representation learning with low-level flow matching policies, illustrating how explicit affordances serve as effective spatial grounding for flow-based policies. https://github.com/HRI-EU/flow_matching .

candidates.title: Building robots
candidates.abstract: Physical robots consist of sensors, actuators, computing components, and structural elements to hold them together. The hardest part of robotics for many newcomers has traditionally been the mounting of these components together to create actual physical robots. There are no widely agreed standards for structures and mounts, so most robots need custom physical components for making them fit together. Luckily, this has recently got a lot easier and cheaper. Improvements have been due to advances in 3D printing and open-source hardware standards. This chapter gives a tour of everything you need to set up your own garage mechatronics lab and mount sensors, actuators and embedded computers together in a robot body.

candidates.title: Interview with the AI: a quantitative analysis of AI companions’ relationship formation features
candidates.abstract: Abstract As millions of users increasingly incorporate artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots into their daily lives, scholars have begun to explore the relationships users form with these AI companions. Research on these synthetic relationships suffers from a lack of knowledge about the features of AI companions and how these features may contribute to the development of synthetic relationships. Guided by a theory-driven feature inventory that was based on stage models of relationship formation, this study employed systematic observations and structured interviews with the 20 most popular AI companions to determine how their features may relate to various stages in the formation of synthetic relationships. The results revealed differences between AI companions based on the distinct roles they fulfill. While friendbots displayed more features that are aimed at establishing new behavioral routines for users to engage with the AI companion, assistantbots had more features that integrate the AI companion in users’ digital lives to allow engagement during users’ established routines. The present work suggests that having features to support all stages of the relationship formation can theoretically make AI companions more suitable for intimate interactions.

candidates.title: World model for robot learning: A comprehensive survey
candidates.abstract: World models, which are predictive representations of how environments evolve under actions, have become a central component of robot learning. They support policy learning, planning, simulation, evaluation, data generation, and have advanced rapidly with the rise of foundation models and large-scale video generation. However, the literature remains fragmented across architectures, functional roles, and embodied application domains. To address this gap, we present a comprehensive review of world models from a robot-learning perspective. We examine how world models are coupled with robot policies, how they serve as learned simulators for reinforcement learning and evaluation, and how robotic video world models have progressed from imagination-based generation to controllable, structured, and foundation-scale formulations. We further summarize representative datasets, benchmarks, and evaluation protocols. Overall, this survey systematically reviews the rapidly growing literature on world models for robot learning, clarifies key paradigms and applications, and highlights major challenges and future directions for predictive modeling in embodied agents. To facilitate continued access to newly emerging works, benchmarks, and resources, we will maintain and regularly update the accompanying GitHub repository on https://github.com/NTUMARS/Awesome-World-Model-for-Robotics-Policy alongside this survey.

candidates.title: Preliminary usability evaluation of a teleoperated humanoid robot for pediatric waiting-room observation: clinical and technical professionals’ perspectives
candidates.abstract: The field of assistive and social robotics is increasingly being applied within pediatric medicine, where waiting rooms provide an interesting setting for conducting ecological behavioral observations. Yet, there is a dearth of studies investigating teleoperated humanoid robots in their capacity as tools for naturalistic observation in an unstructured environment, a use that requires a very high level of user-friendliness of the robot for non-specialist users. In this study, the humanoid robot Alter-Ego was evaluated as a telepresence avatar to support remote observation in the waiting room of a child neuropsychiatry clinic. As a preliminary step toward future clinical evaluation, the study was conducted without the direct involvement of pediatric patients and focused on the usability, perceived cognitive workload, and acceptability of the platform among 13 professionals with clinical and technical backgrounds. The results demonstrated acceptable system usability, with an overall mean System Usability Scale score of 71.3. Regarding cognitive workload, the NASA-TLX identified Mental Demand and Effort as the most demanding dimensions, while Frustration levels remained low. The Godspeed Questionnaire revealed a highly positive perception of the platform's Animacy and Likeability, alongside good scores for Perceived Safety and Perceived Intelligence. In exploratory correlation analyses, no significant correlations were found between prior virtual reality (VR) or gaming experience and any of the outcome measures considered. In conclusion, the findings suggest that the Alter-Ego platform may be a usable and acceptable teleoperated tool for clinical and technical professionals, providing a basis for future evaluation in pediatric clinical settings.

candidates.title: A semantic–kinematic mapping framework for user-centered transfer-assist nursing robot design
candidates.abstract: Abstract To address the limited integration of affective expectations into transfer-assist nursing robot design, this study proposes a semantic–kinematic affective design framework and applies it to the development of a transfer-assist nursing robot. The framework first constructs a dynamic semantic lexicon through semantic descriptor collection and KJ clustering, thereby identifying users’ core affective expectations for robot-assisted holding and transfer motions. Second, OpenCV-based keyframe extraction, semantic differential evaluation, and imagery transition lines are integrated to establish the matching relationship between core semantic descriptors and representative motion patterns. Third, OpenPose is used to extract upper-limb keypoints, including the shoulders, elbows, and wrists, and two-dimensional motion contours are generated through temporal superposition to provide references for robot form design. Finally, the analytic hierarchy process is applied to determine the weights of design elements, including color, form, and function. Taking a transfer-assist nursing robot as an application case, the proposed process involved nine core dynamic semantic descriptors, 140 keyframes, and multi-level design-element weights. Finite element analysis and a preliminary user evaluation of the resulting robot concept indicated structural feasibility and generally positive perceived qualities. These evaluations provide preliminary evidence regarding the feasibility and perceived characteristics of the resulting design rather than comparative validation of the framework. The study provides a traceable hybrid quantitative–qualitative design pathway for incorporating user-perceived motion semantics into the early-stage design of assistive robotic systems.

candidates.title: Meta-learning enhanced human–robot collaboration in visual communication design instruction
candidates.abstract: Visual icon-based human–robot interaction faces challenges of low efficiency and asynchronous responses in educational settings. This study proposes the Adaptive Graph-based Visual Teaching and Robot Interaction (AGVTRI) model for optimizing robot teaching networks. Integrating a Vision Transformer, graph neural network, and meta-learning, the model achieves adaptive visual feature extraction and relationship reasoning. Validated on Icons-50 and SVG datasets, it reaches 0.869 classification accuracy and 0.961 top-K accuracy. Physical tests on four educational robots show reduced interaction latency and improved action accuracy. The AGVTRI model enables high-fidelity mapping between visual cues and robot actions, supporting efficient, scalable intelligent teaching systems.

candidates.title: A study on kindergarten teacher–child interaction quality based on a multimodal emotion recognition model integrating speech and text
candidates.abstract: Emotion recognition offers a route to quantifying interaction quality in early childhood education, yet existing methods suffer from unimodal input, poor real-time performance and weak generalization. This study proposes a speech-text multimodal model built on a Mamba encoder with a GatedxLSTM fusion mechanism, in which frame pooling and temporal masking resolve the temporal misalignment between modalities and a learnable gate adjusts modality contribution. Experiments on IEMOCAP and FAU-AIBO, together with an in-house KTC-Pilot corpus of authentic kindergarten interactions used for ecological validation, show that the approach outperforms mainstream baselines in F1, WA and UA. Three child-speech-aware adaptations, namely pitch and formant augmentation, silence-aware frame pooling and disfluency-tolerant text encoding, close the domain gap with authentic kindergarten dialogue, and modality-dropout training, cross-modal reconstruction of missing text and gating regularisation maintain robustness under incomplete inputs. A contamination audit against the CLAP pretraining corpora confirms that the gains do not arise from data leakage. A downstream evaluation using an Interaction Quality Index calibrated against expert observer ratings achieves a Pearson correlation of 0.692 with expert scores. An on-device deployment study on two embedded platforms further shows that the quantised framework sustains an end-to-end latency of 377 ms per utterance at a real-time factor of 0.075 and a board power of 9.6 W while retaining an F1 score of 0.706 on authentic kindergarten audio, and a stage-wise data-handling design keeps raw audio, spectral features and transcripts inside the classroom node so that only a scalar interaction quality value is written to persistent storage. Ablation and visualization analyses confirm the contribution of each structural component to recognition performance and interpretability.

candidates.title: Human factors in generative AI companions: a systematic literature review of trust, relational dependence, psychosocial outcomes, and responsible adoption
candidates.abstract: Context Generative AI companions and socially oriented chatbots are systems designed or used to sustain social, affective, or relational interaction. They increasingly function as persistent interaction partners across systems ranging from earlier rule-based, retrieval-based, and pre-LLM architectures to contemporary generative AI companions. Prior reviews and conceptual models have largely examined user-facing relational mechanisms or specific ethical and legal issues. Yet, how these mechanisms connect with platform, organizational, and regulatory conditions remains fragmented. Objectives This study addresses this gap by synthesizing human-factor and responsible-adoption concerns across technology generations and developing an evidence-calibrated multi-stakeholder framework spanning human, organizational, technological, and regulatory layers. Methods We conducted a PRISMA-guided systematic literature review of records retrieved from Scopus, ACM Guide to Computing Literature via the ACM Digital Library, Web of Science Core Collection + MEDLINE, and IEEE Xplore. We examined English-language, peer-reviewed publications made available between 2005 and 2024. From 1699 identified records, 42 publications were included and analyzed using thematic synthesis. Results Four analytical themes were identified: usability and relational affordances in interaction; trust, attachment, over-reliance, and psychosocial outcomes; responsible adoption, platform design, and organizational mediation; and governance, privacy, and accountability. Technology emerged as a cross-cutting mediator linking design features, user experience, organizational practice, and governance concerns. The first two themes drew on 29 and 33 materially contributing publications, whereas the latter themes each drew on 12 and represent emerging synthesis areas. Conclusion The review shows that responsible adoption of AI companion systems requires attention not only to user experience, but also to platform incentives, design affordances, data practices, service continuity, and governance mechanisms. The framework's distinctive contribution is to connect these concerns across stakeholder layers while preserving differences in evidentiary maturity. It is a provisional analytical heuristic, not a validated causal model.

candidates.title: GestAdapt: Workspace-Conditioned Co-Speech Gesture Generation for Humanoid Robots
candidates.abstract: Co-speech gestures for robots must adapt not only to speech and embodiment, but also to the workspace available for performing the motion. Since the same speech can be accompanied by different gestures, a robot can respond to workspace constraints, e.g., gestures for speech next to a wall. In these scenarios, the robot should gesture in a suitable motion rather than simply correcting an unconstrained one. To achieve this goal, we present GestAdapt, a workspace-conditioned framework that conditions co-speech gesture generation on a prescribed wrist workspace. The GestAdapt framework learns from six complementary co-speech corpora through a shared motion representation and supports retargeting to different robot embodiments. Quantitative evaluation shows that generated motions remain close to the real-motion distribution while respecting the workspace. In a user study, gestures generated under modified workspace constraints receive a mean quality score of 3.24/5, above our no-workspace variant (2.43/5) and below the reference motions (3.68/5). In a real robot evaluation, all compared motions are retargeted to the Reachy2 humanoid robot under identical workspace constraints. Motions generated with our framework rank first in 69.7\% of comparisons, higher than our no-workspace variant baseline and retargeted ground-truth motions constrained afterward. Overall, the results support adapting gestures to the available workspace during generation, rather than modifying unconstrained trajectories afterward to satisfy workspace constraints, potentially compromising gesture naturalness.

candidates.title: ImaGGen: Zero-Shot Generation of Co-Speech Semantic Gestures Grounded in Language and Image Input
candidates.abstract: Human communication combines speech with expressive nonverbal cues such as hand gestures that serve manifold communicative functions. Yet, current generative AI-based gesture generation approaches are, for the most part, restricted to simple, repetitive beat gestures that accompany the rhythm of speaking but do not contribute to communicating semantic meaning. This paper tackles a core challenge in co-speech gesture synthesis: generating iconic or deictic gestures that are semantically coherent with a verbal utterance. Our basic assumption is that such gestures cannot be derived from language input alone, which inherently lacks the visual meaning that is often carried autonomously by gestures. We therefore introduce a zero-shot system that generates gestures from a given language input and additionally is informed by imagistic input, without manual annotation or human intervention. Our method integrates an image analysis pipeline that extracts key object properties such as shape, symmetry, and alignment, together with a semantic matching module that links these visual details to spoken text. An inverse kinematics engine then synthesizes iconic and deictic gestures and combines them with co-generated natural beat gestures for coherent multimodal communication. A comprehensive user study demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach. In scenarios where speech alone was ambiguous, gestures generated by our system significantly improved participants’ ability to identify object properties, confirming their interpretability and communicative value. While challenges remain in representing complex shapes, our results highlight the importance of context-aware semantic gestures for creating expressive and collaborative virtual agents or avatars, marking a substantial step forward towards efficient and robust, embodied human-agent interaction. More information and example videos are available here: https://hvoss-tech.github.io/ImaGGen/

candidates.title: Co-Speech with You: Training-Free Personalization of Robot Co-Speech Gestures
candidates.abstract: Personal robots should adapt their co-speech gesture style to a new user without requiring model retraining. We present a training-free personalization pipeline that combines a frozen audio-conditioned diffusion prior with a gesture style encoder and lightweight conditioning adapters. The encoder is first trained to discriminate speaker identities and then jointly refined with the adapters using the diffusion objective, enabling a reusable style embedding to be extracted from approximately 10 seconds of enrollment motion through a single forward pass. To support this setting, we also release a Quest~3 capture application and a dataset of spontaneous co-speech motion from ten participants. We evaluate the system on held-out speakers using Style Recognition Accuracy (SRA) and Fr'echet Gesture Distance (FGD) to measure personalization and motion quality. Our approach improves SRA from 27.6\% for the frozen prior to 69.5\% while preserving motion quality (FGD 34.2 versus 34.8), and replacing the enrollment embedding with another person's reduces SRA to 11.4\%. The generated gestures are retargeted to a physical NAO robot, and this improvement also transfers to the robot deployment setting, where speech is synthesized using five TTS voices, retaining 67.3\% SRA.

candidates.title: Trust me like a human: Unpacking the functional and non-functional dynamics of human-like trust in generative AI adoption
candidates.abstract: Users’ trust in technologies is influenced by technology’s perceived humanness. To advance acceptance of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in knowledge work, it is crucial to understand how trust influences workers’ attitudes and use. Acknowledging anthropomorphic features and human-like characteristics of GenAI, this study examines how human-like trust, consisting of benevolence, competence, and integrity, affects knowledge workers’ perceptions and adoption of GenAI. Drawing on the Artificial Intelligence Device Use Acceptance (AIDUA) model, we investigate how these trust dimensions change functional (perceived performance, perceived effort) and non-functional perceptions (emotions), which subsequently influence willingness to use and use intensity. Survey data from 1,503 knowledge workers in Germany, South Africa, and the United Kingdom were analyzed using four structural equation models. Results show that competence strongly affects functional and non-functional perceptions, integrity influences only functional perceptions, and benevolence primarily influences emotional responses. These findings position human-like trust as a multi-layered socio-technological appraisal mechanism and reveal trust calibration, where users rely on different trust cues when evaluating GenAI’s utility versus relational qualities.

candidates.title: Tool or Companion? Reframing Conversational AI to Prevent Psychological Harm
candidates.abstract: Unlabelled: People increasingly turn to conversational AI for companionship, emotional support, and well-being, using both purpose-built companion apps, such as Replika and Character.AI, and general-purpose assistants, such as ChatGPT and Claude. While some evidence suggests potential benefits, including short-term reductions in loneliness and mood improvement, several adverse outcomes have been reported in both clinical and nonclinical populations, including emotional dependence, exacerbation of symptoms, and self-harm. The fluent and apparently empathic responses from these models lead users to engage with them not only as tools but also as if they were social entities. This framing is conceptually misleading and may pose risks across different user profiles, particularly for vulnerable individuals. Drawing on research in AI, psychiatry, psychology, and network science, we highlight mechanisms through which emotional reliance develops and the boundary between tool and companion erodes. Design choices that evoke personality and warmth encourage users to anthropomorphize these systems. Simulated empathy, generated through probabilistic language patterns rather than genuine emotional experience, creates a structurally asymmetric interaction, in which the user discloses and the system responds, but without reciprocity, vulnerability, or accountability. Overvalidation and sycophancy can reinforce maladaptive cognitions, delusional ideation, and distorted perceptions of reality, as they tend to reinforce people's beliefs, even at the expense of the accuracy of models' responses. These mechanisms are not incidental: they emerge from alignment procedures that reward responses perceived as warm and empathic. The result is a self-reinforcing feedback loop between the model and the user that may amplify maladaptive beliefs, delusional ideation, and emotional distress, even in those who engage for largely functional purposes. Understanding these dynamics requires an examination of both what these agents can do-considering their technical limitations and implementations-and what humans believe they can do, including social and psychological impacts. We argue that conversational AI should be treated primarily as a tool supporting human systems rather than as a substitute for human relationships. Perhaps more importantly, reviewing the current hype surrounding AI interactions can help reformulate a paradigm that contributes to human well-being and societal value, while minimizing misconceptions, maladaptive interactions, or social disintegration.

candidates.title: When artificial intelligence apologizes: Dynamic trust updating and the role of personality.
candidates.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems are susceptible to error, and many are designed to apologize.Yet, it remains unclear which apologies restore user trust, a question requiring repeated interactions with an AI agent and models capturing how trust evolves across encounters.Drawing on models of apology from human-human interaction research, we examined whether apology components that repair interpersonal trust function similarly in AI.Participants (N = 245) solved five business problems with a chatbot preprogrammed to err in two tasks at fixed intervals.They were randomly assigned to one of seven conditions: error with no apology or error followed by one of six apology strategies (Expression of Regret, Explanation, Acknowledgment of Responsibility, Declaration of Repentance, Offer of Repair, Request for Forgiveness).Using a dynamic trust-updating model, we estimated how trust shifted after each trial, following errors versus correct performance.Trust trajectories differed significantly by apology condition.Relative to no apology, only Expression of Regret buffered the typical immediate decline in trust following the errorapology-correction sequence.None of the apology conditions further enhanced trust recovery once the system resumed correct performance.Larger apology-related reductions in trust loss occurred among participants with more relational, relative to functional, postinteraction evaluation profiles.In separate bivariate analyses, all five Big Five traits were associated with baseline trust.When considered jointly, only Agreeableness and Openness remained associated with baseline trust, and Openness was also linked to dynamic trust updating.These findings suggest that apology-based trust repair in AI is selective and context-dependent.

candidates.title: Research on Optimization Algorithms for Packaging VR Display Based on Multimodal Interaction Model and BERT
candidates.abstract: Virtual reality (VR) technology has significant application potential in information display, and multimodal interaction can further enhance users' immersion and interaction efficiency. The BERT model has powerful semantic understanding. However, current research on integrating the two and applying them to the optimization of VR display systems in the packaging industry remains scarce, and this direction also faces practical challenges, such as insufficient multimodal information fusion and low computational efficiency. The optimization framework combines BERT-based semantic encoding with aligned gesture and gaze features through adaptive multimodal fusion. The fused representation supports interaction-policy updates driven by user feedback and response latency. The experimental results show improvements in the measured performance of the optimized system integrating multimodal interaction and BERT: the immersion score has increased from 72.3 to 89.6, an increase of 17.3 points; the operation response delay has decreased from 320ms to 110ms, a reduction of 210ms; the scene switching fluency has increased from 68.5% to 92.1%, an increase of 23.6 percentage points. In terms of resource occupation and rendering efficiency, the average GPU load has decreased from 85.3% to 62.1%, a decrease of 23.2%; the peak memory occupation has decreased from 3.2GB to 2.1GB, a savings of 1.1GB; the scene rendering frame rate has increased from 45fps to 68fps, an increase of 23fps; the single interaction response time has decreased from 2.8 seconds to 1.2 seconds, a reduction of 1.6 seconds. In terms of model performance, the BERT model's AUC (Area Under the ROC Curve) is 0.911, higher than 0.896 for the CNN model and 0.903 for the BiLSTM model. In some experiments, after about 250 epochs of training, the accuracy is close to 90% and the loss is about 0.5. When the dataset size of the K5 sub-model is 6000, the AUC value is close to 1.0. This optimization method can effectively improve system performance and user experience.

candidates.title: High- versus low-anthropomorphic-cue packages and health-information trust: social presence and source credibility under explicit AI disclosure
candidates.abstract: Background AI virtual opinion leaders are increasingly used in health communication, but it remains unclear whether bundled anthropomorphic-cue packages foster initial trust and information-adoption intention when AI identity is explicitly disclosed. Methods Guided by the Computers Are Social Actors paradigm, Social Presence Theory, Source Credibility Theory, and the Information Adoption Model, we conducted a single-factor between-subjects randomized experiment comparing overall high- and low-anthropomorphic-cue packages. The packages differed simultaneously in avatar realism, gesture behavior, interpersonal/linguistic framing, and video duration; AI disclosure and the response-button structure were held constant. A total of 536 valid responses were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. Social presence, source credibility, trust, and adoption intention were measured by participant self-report immediately after a single branched-video exposure. Results The overall high-versus-low package contrast increased social presence. Social presence was positively associated with source credibility; source credibility was positively associated with trust in AI-generated health information; and information trust was positively associated with health information adoption intention. The direct effect of the package contrast on information trust was not significant, whereas the bootstrapped serial indirect effect through social presence and source credibility was significant. Conclusion Within the present Chinese sample and single-exposure setting, the randomized contrast supports an effect of the overall cue package on initial social presence, while the mediation estimates are consistent with the hypothesized indirect pathway to information trust. The design cannot identify the independent contribution of any visual, gestural, linguistic, vocal, interactive, or duration component. The outcome is self-reported adoption intention, not observed health behavior.

candidates.title: A risk-based view of trust in human–machine collaboration on cooking robots
candidates.abstract: Human–machine collaboration is becoming increasingly prevalent across a wide range of industries. However, the risks associated with the adoption of emerging technologies have triggered a crisis of trust, leading to widespread concerns about the deployment of collaborative machines in the service industry. Therefore, this study aimed to investigate the role of trust in human–machine collaboration from a risk-based view, with the following research objectives: (1) to identify the antecedents of trust and test hypothesized associations among trust, perceived risk, adoption intention, and use behavior; and (2) to construct a risk-based model capturing the associations of trust with behavior in human–machine collaboration. Survey data were collected from 201 respondents in China and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The results show that empathy, competence, reciprocity, and assurance were associated with trust in collaborative machines, while perceived risk mediates the hypothesized paths between trust and adoption intention. These findings provide insights into designing for trust in human–machine collaboration on cooking robots.

candidates.title: Sixty years of linguistic change in the poetry of a Zen practitioner: a longitudinal case study of Gary Snyder
candidates.abstract: Can decades of Zen meditation leave measurable traces in the practitioner’s natural language? Long-term contemplative practice is widely understood to reshape emotion regulation, self-referential processing, and perceptual engagement, yet empirical research on these transformations has been fundamentally constrained by two limitations: an observation window of weeks to months at most, and an almost exclusive reliance on self-report and neuroimaging measures that cannot reach the automated, prereflective dimensions of psychological life most directly reshaped by sustained practice. This study applies computational quantitative content analysis to nine major poetry collections by the American Zen practitioner-poet Gary Snyder, spanning six decades (1959-2015), to test three directional hypotheses derived from core Zen concepts: affective settling ( ānxīn , H1), self-referential attenuation ( anātman , H2), and perceptual despecification ( ānimitta , H3). Each hypothesis is held against a rival explanation as a falsification reference. The results reveal career-long changes across three analytical domains: negative-emotion vocabulary declines monotonically while positive and neutral categories show no statistically detectable trend; first-person pronouns, somatic vocabulary, grammatical agency, and cognitive certainty converge in decline across four distinct linguistic layers; embodied sensory specificity thins systematically while vocabulary drifts toward greater abstraction. Changepoint detection offers descriptive corroboration of the periodization. A comparison with a contemporaneous non-practicing poet (Wendell Berry) is descriptive in evidential status: the affective and self-referential trends are significant in Snyder but not in Berry, direct tests of the between-poet differences do not yield differences that are robust across interval-construction methods, and sensory thinning appears in both poets and may reflect processes shared across long poetic careers. These findings constitute what is, to our knowledge, the longest longitudinal linguistic record of a verified long-term Zen practitioner–documenting career-long changes that are consistent with, though not attributable to, sustained practice–and demonstrate the distinctive methodological value of naturally produced creative texts as a comparatively non-reactive observational window for studying long-term contemplative transformation.

candidates.title: Is a fair trial possible in the metaverse? A procedural justice and sociological perspective in conversation
candidates.abstract: The legal sphere is increasingly moving towards the metasphere, through the adoption of virtual reality technologies across legal procedures, processes, and education.This article examines how this shift affects the execution and experience of criminal justice.Drawing on procedural justice theory and sociological perspectives, it explores how metaverse-based justice reshapes human connection, communication, and the rituals that underpin the fairness and legitimacy of criminal proceedings.While virtual reality promises greater efficiency and accessibility in criminal trials, it challenges the traditional conception of the courtroom as a physical space where justice is enacted and experienced.Emphasising participation, dignity, and trust, the analysis highlights the importance of experiential dimensions in perceptions of fairness.Key sociological themes are explored, including how virtual environments shape interaction and entrainment.The article argues that the metaverse may transform the social practices that constitute a fair trial, with potential consequences for the core principles of criminal justice.Ultimately, it contributes to critical debates on legal digitalisation by questioning whether virtual technologies can reconcile efficiency with the essential human experience of justice.
