candidates.title: An open-set hybrid CNN-TCN network for human action recognition with unknown action rejection in collaborative robot workspaces
candidates.abstract: Introduction: Open-set recognition capability is becoming necessary for collaborative robots because actual shop-floor dynamics do not always correspond to the fixed action classes used during training. Misclassification of unknown human motions may lead to inappropriate robot responses, whereas reliable rejection enables safer supervisory control. Methods: An open-set human action recognition framework is developed by combining a spatial Convolutional Neural Network encoder with a Temporal Convolutional Network-based temporal aggregation module and an unknown-action rejection gate based on open-set scoring. The framework is evaluated on the NTU RGB+D 120 dataset using cross-subject and cross-view protocols with held-out action classes. Results: The proposed framework achieves 93.20% and 91.00% top-1 accuracy under cross-subject and cross-view evaluation, respectively, with corresponding Macro-F1 scores of 88.40% and 86.20%. For open-set detection, it achieves an AUROC of 0.938 and an AUPR of 0.750, with a 5.00% false acceptance rate for unknown actions and a 91.82% true known-action acceptance rate. The system operates at 15.0 ms per window and 66 fps on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX 16 GB, with a model size of 42 MB. Discussion: The results demonstrate that calibrated unknown-action rejection can improve safety-aware human action recognition while retaining practical real-time performance for collaborative robot workspaces.

candidates.title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) Can't Feel Me: Lower Perceived AI Perspective–Taking Impedes Human–AI Cooperation
candidates.abstract: ABSTRACT As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly autonomous, its interactions with humans increasingly resemble social relationships, giving rise to a novel form of cooperation—human–AI teaming. Drawing on social cognition theory, the present research examines how individuals’ perceived AI perspective–taking shapes their willingness to cooperate. Across five studies, we find that individuals are generally reluctant to cooperate with AI possessing partial decision‐making authority (Studies 1 and 2), and this reluctance is shaped by perceived AI perspective‐taking (Studies 3 and 4). When AI agents appear to accurately—or even slightly overestimate—the thoughts and feelings of individuals experiencing unfair situations, perceived AI perspective–taking increases, thereby enhancing their willingness to cooperate with AI (Study 5). These findings extend perspective–taking research from human–human to human–AI contexts, highlighting that cooperation with AI depends not only on instrumental outcomes but also on social–cognitive inferences about being understood, and suggesting that psychologically anthropomorphic design may foster more effective human–AI interaction.

Preschool children develop scientific inquiry skills through STEM based investigations
candidates.abstract: Curiosity-driven exploration plays a fundamental role in young children’s early encounters with science and supports the development of scientific inquiry skills in early childhood education. In recent years, constructivist and child-centered approaches have increasingly emphasized the importance of engaging children in active investigation processes. Within this perspective, project-based learning offers meaningful opportunities for children to explore real-life phenomena, ask questions, and construct knowledge through hands-on experiences. The present study aimed to examine how a project-based STEM learning process can support preschool children’s scientific inquiry skills through an investigation of ants as a natural phenomenon that emerged from children’s curiosity. The study was designed as a qualitative case study. The participants consisted of 21 preschool children aged 60–72 months attending a kindergarten in the city center of Uşak, Türkiye. Data were collected during the 2020–2021 academic year through structured observations, interviews conducted before and after the project implementation, and document analysis, including observation notes and visual materials documenting children’s activities. The project was implemented following the three phases of the project approach: initiation, fieldwork, and finalization. The findings indicate that the project-based STEM process encouraged children to ask questions, make observations, develop explanations, and engage in collaborative inquiry while exploring ants. The results also suggest that integrating natural phenomena into project-based STEM activities can effectively support preschool children’s curiosity, critical thinking, and early scientific inquiry skills. These findings highlight the importance of inquiry-oriented and project-based learning environments in early childhood science education and provide practical implications for educators seeking to foster young children’s engagement with scientific exploration.

candidates.title: Giving robots the intelligence to work beyond Earth
candidates.abstract: Giving robots the intelligence to work beyond Earth SpaceR develops artificial intelligence that enables robots to explore, service, assemble and operate autonomously across planetary and orbital missions. The future of space exploration will not be limited by launch capability – it will be defined by robotic intelligence. As humanity prepares for a permanent presence on the Moon and a rapidly expanding orbital economy, robots must become capable of making complex decisions, adapting to uncertain environments and safely interacting with the physical world with minimal human supervision. At the University of Luxembourg, the Space Robotics Research Group (SpaceR) is developing the artificial intelligence (AI) that will power this new generation of autonomous space systems. Since its foundation in 2020, the group has rapidly established itself as one of Europe’s leading centres for AI in space robotics, securing more than €12.5m in research funding, delivering over 30 competitive research projects, publishing more than 130 scientific papers, and building unique experimental facilities dedicated to advancing robotic autonomy beyond Earth.

candidates.abstract: Ursula Damm is a German artist and professor known for her work at the intersection of interactive digital art, urban space, and ecology.She holds the chair for Media Environments at the Bauhaus-Universität Weimar, where her projects explore both nature and technological systems.Using contemporary technologies, her installations serve as mediators between the habitats of humans, animals, and plants.

candidates.title: Autonomous robotic operation controlled by wave-based neuromorphic hardware
candidates.abstract: Abstract Equipping robots with a physical, brain-inspired computing unit is a key step towards achieving true autonomy in intelligent machines; however, the practical realization of such neuromorphic hardware remains a major challenge. Because both software- and hardware-based spiking neural network approaches demand substantial training and energy consumption, an architecturally simple neuromorphic platform is required to enable scalable and energy-efficient robotics. Here, we experimentally demonstrate robotic control driven by a neuromorphic hardware based on physical wave interactions. Using a water-based experimental system that provides direct visual access to wave-network dynamics, we establish a wave-based reservoir computing framework that achieves near-perfect accuracy in robotic vehicle obstacle recognition, followed by real-time autonomous motion with obstacle avoidance controlled entirely by this wave-based hardware. Through micromagnetic simulations, we extend this concept to electrically excited spin waves in a magnetic nanodevice operating at gigahertz frequencies, outlining an approach toward solid-state robotic chips based on wave computing. These results position wave-based computation as a scalable and energy-efficient alternative to conventional digital neuromorphic architectures for next-generation intelligent machines.

candidates.title: Remote Actuation of Concentric Tube Robots Using Torque Cables
candidates.abstract: The precision and flexibility of Concentric Tube Robots (CTRs) makes them well-suited for delicate surgeries and complex tasks in constrained environments, such as minimally invasive procedures. However, traditional CTRs can be bulky, as actuation typically requires multiple motors directly connected to the individual tubes. To reduce the system’s footprint, this paper proposes and evaluates remote actuation (from 1 m away) of concentric tubes using torque cables. First, we investigate the theoretical framework influencing torque transmission. Second, on a two-tube, balanced pair CTR prototype, we demonstrate the method’s performance in terms of tracing target positions and overall teleoperation ability. This study highlights the advantages and challenges of remote actuation, addressing key considerations and trade-offs when implementing this approach, and, critically, allows for miniaturising CTRs to deploy them closer to the target site without being limited by bulky actuation units.

candidates.title: Material minds: mapping care and learning across everyday objects
candidates.abstract: What can mapping care and learning across everyday material objects tell us about the human mind? Traditional perspectives have often treated objects as passive tools valued mainly for their utility or market worth. In contrast, psychological and cultural research has emphasized the psychological and identity-related significance of material objects. Building on prior human-object interaction (HOI) research, this study examines care and learning as two previously identified psychological dimensions characterizing meaningful engagement with material artefacts. Using a large-scale online survey of 3441 Japanese adults, we examined how object-related characteristics—such as ownership, shared memories, subjective irreplaceability, mental concentration, instrumentality, perceived monetary value, and difficulty of use—were associated with care and learning. Cluster analysis of 39 object types identified six distinct profiles of care and learning, indicating systematic variation across object types. Ownership, irreplaceability, and mental concentration showed positive adjusted associations with both care and learning, while shared memories were more strongly associated with learning. In contrast, usage duration and frequency were largely unrelated to either dimension, indicating that temporal exposure alone was not closely associated with care or learning. By mapping patterns of care and learning across diverse everyday objects, this study extends the HOI framework and provides an empirical basis for connecting it with research on the extended self. Because the study was cross-sectional, the findings should be interpreted as associations rather than causal effects. Overall, the results highlight the psychological significance of everyday material artefacts beyond their utility or market value and support closer attention to how people experience and relate to objects in contemporary material culture.

candidates.title: The Digital Transparent
candidates.abstract: In the 2010s, digital platforms swiftly became the dominant way to disseminate media content, promising to make communication transparent in ways that print, cinema and broadcast never could. The Digital Transparent critically interrogates this claim, arguing that while platforms introduce new transparencies, they also create opacities intrinsic to their technology and architecture. Using Michel Foucault’s concept of the dispositif, the book demonstrates that transparency arrangements are always selective, partial and strategically constructed. It argues that transparency functions both as an opening up of the platform and as a mechanism that enables platforms to govern. Through dispositif analysis of two key transparency devices—the dashboard and the transparency centre—the book examines YouTube, SoundCloud, Facebook and X.com/Twitter using textual analysis, interface analysis and interviews with YouTubers. The Digital Transparent is essential reading for students and scholars in media studies, offering a historical perspective on digital platforms that reveals what is genuinely new and what continues from earlier media. It will appeal to those interested in Foucault’s work and its application to contemporary media, researchers in transparency studies seeking critical perspectives on communication and distribution, and platform scholars focused on governance, creative practices and regulation.

candidates.title: BLUEMIRA : a modular, open-source framework for designing tokamak fusion reactors
candidates.abstract: Abstract As efforts across the world to deliver fusion power enter their respective conceptual design stages, many begin to encounter the difficulties of generating complete designs, evaluating them, performing trade-off studies, and comparing different alternatives. Many organisations successfully use fusion reactor systems codes with low-fidelity formulations of the critical physics and engineering aspects to inform the initial design stage and steer them towards a region of the design space they consider attractive, but struggle to explore the design space in more depth. This work is an overview of the open-source tokamak reactor design framework, BLUEMIRA , built from the BLUEPRINT (Coleman and McIntosh 2019 Fusion Eng. Des. 139 26–38; Coleman 2021 Thesis, University of Cambridge) and MIRA (Franza 2019 Development and validation of a computational tool for fusion reactors system analysis; Franza F. et al 2022 Nucl. Fusion 62 076042) codes, which goes beyond the ‘classical’ systems code paradigm and enables the user to parameterise their reactor designs at higher fidelity. Reactor design workflows ranging from 0-D ‘radial build’ design, equilibrium design, to 3-D CAD and automated neutronics analyses can be run within minutes. We present the functionality implemented in the BLUEMIRA code and demonstrate its application to the conceptual design of a conventional aspect ratio fusion reactor, performing an indicative design study over aspect ratio and number of toroidal field coils.

candidates.title: A large‐scale open‐source σ‐profile database for COSMO ‐ SAC
candidates.abstract: Abstract We present an open‐source σ‐profile database encompassing 361,583 neutral organic molecules. The σ‐profiles were computed using density‐functional theory in the conductor‐screening limit with the open‐source PySCF package, using PM6‐optimized geometries from PubChemQC. This database is 162 times larger than the reference of Bell et al. (2261 molecules) and 6.8 times larger than CHAOS (53,091 molecules). To recalibrate COSMO‐SAC for PySCF‐derived σ‐profiles, we performed a sequential three‐stage reparametrization of the five exchange‐energy parameters using 24,522 infinite‐dilution activity coefficient data from the NIST/TRC ThermoData Engine. Validation across three independent benchmarks demonstrated accuracy comparable to the established DMol3‐based reference. The infinite‐dilution activity coefficient yielded an RMSE of 0.898 versus 0.961 on 9748 data points. Vapor–liquid equilibria showed a mean pressure deviation of 3.12% versus 3.92% on 12 binary systems. Solid–liquid equilibria produced an RMSE of 0.412 versus 0.458 on 22 solute–solvent pairs. The database, parameters, and code are openly available.

candidates.title: A short review of open-source malware datasets and their implications for quantum machine learning
candidates.abstract: The rapid development of quantum machine learning (QML) has created new opportunities for malware detection and classification. However, the effectiveness of QML-based malware research depends strongly on the availability and suitability of open-source malware datasets. Although many publicly accessible malware datasets have been designed for classical machine learning, their features and limitations have not been systematically scrutinised on quantum computing grounds. This short review provides a structured overview of publicly available open-source malware datasets: EMBER (Endgame Malware BEnchmark for Research), DREBIN Android malware dataset, CIC-MalMem-2022 (Canadian Institute for Cybersecurity Malware Memory Analysis Dataset 2022), and VirusShare, and evaluates their suitability for quantum machine learning applications. The datasets are analysed based on data modality, feature representation, mode of labelling, and accessibility. Key research issues are identified, including high dimensionality, class imbalance, uncertainty of labels, and dataset bias. Particular attention is given to limitations posed by near-term quantum devices, such as qubit availability, circuit depth restrictions, and data encoding overhead. Among the reviewed datasets, DREBIN offers the most favourable characteristics for near-term QML experimentation. Its sparse binary feature structure, after reduction to a 126-feature subset or via principal component analysis (PCA) to 15 - 50 components, yields compact vectors compatible with current qubit constraints. EMBER and VirusShare present the greatest encoding challenges owing to their very high dimensionality and lack of standardised feature representations. Angle encoding and hybrid quantum-classical approaches are identified as the most practical encoding strategies for current NISQ (Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum) devices. A five-criterion evaluation framework, covering feature dimensionality, encoding feasibility, dataset size, label quality, and preprocessing requirements, is proposed to guide dataset selection. The findings underscore the urgent need for purpose-built benchmark datasets designed with quantum hardware constraints in mind.
